items.title: Hands-On Tasks
items.text:
Participants may ask event supervisors for details of the internal wiring of any breadboards tasks.

The hands-on tasks, of stations, may include but are not limited to:

  1. Determine the value of a mystery resistor in a circuit using only voltage measurements

  2. Calculate the power supplied to a circuit.

  3. Given some wires, batteries, resistors; and 2 LEDs, hook them up so the LEDs are equally bright.

  4. Given a USB charger, read the label and provide:

    4a. details of the various output power levels it can provide 4b. calculate how long tt would take to charge a specific battery

  5. Construct a logic circuit to mimic a given truth table.

  6. Troubleshoot a faulty circuit.

  7. Wire a 3-way switch using SPDT switches.

  8. Create a specified equivalent resistance from given individual resistors.

items.title: AI Overview
items.text:
To find the output voltage, analyze the circuit step-by-step using the properties of an ideal op-amp:

  • No current enters or leaves the inverting (\(-\)) and non-inverting (\(+\)) input terminals.

  • The voltage at the inverting terminal equals the voltage at the non-inverting terminal due to the virtual short concept: (\(V_- = V_+\)).

Let the inverting input node of the first op-amp be Node A, the output node of the first op-amp be Node B, and the inverting input node of the second op-amp be Node C.

items.title: Step 1: Find the voltages at the input nodes A and C.
items.text:
For the first op-amp, the non-inverting input is connected to \(1 \text{V}\)

\[ \begin{align} V_\text{A} & = V_\text{+} \\\\ & = 1 \text{V} \end{align} \]

For the second op-amp, the non-inverting input is connected to \(2 \text{V}\)

\[ \begin{align} V_\text{C} & = V_\text{+} \\\\ & = 2 \text{V} \end{align} \]

items.title: Step 2: Apply Kirchhoff's Current Law (KCL) at Node A
items.text:
Sum the currents leaving Node A:

\[ frac{V_\text{A} - 0}{2 \text{k}\Omega} + frac{V_\text{A} - V_\text{B}}{2 \text{k}\Omega} + frac{V_\text{A} - V_\text{C}}{1 \text{k}\Omega} = 0 \]

Substitute the known values (\(V_\text{A} = 1 \text{V}\) and \(V_\text{B} = 2 \text{V}\)):

\[ \begin{align} \frac{1}{2} + \frac{1 - V_\text{B}}{2} + \frac{1 - 2}}{1} & = 0 \\\\ \frac{1}{2} + \frac{1}{2} - \frac{V_\text{B}}{2} - 1 & = 0 \\\\ 1 - \frac{V_\text{B}}{2} - 1 & = 0 \\\\ V_\text{B} = 0 \text{V} \end{align} \]

items.title: Step 3: Apply Kirchhoff's Current Law (KCL) at Node C
items.text:
Summing the currents leaving Node C:

\[ \frac{V_\text{C} - V_\text{A}}{1 k\Omega} + \frac{V_\text{C} - V_\text{B}}{2 k\Omega} + \frac{V_\text{C} - V_0}{2 k\Omega} = 0 \]

Substitute the values (\((V_\text{C} = 2 \text{V}\), \(V_\text{A} = 1 \text{V}\), and \(V_\text{B} = 0 \text{V}\)):

\[ \begin{align} \frac{2 - 1}{1} + \frac{2 - 0}{2} + \frac{2 - V_\text{o}}{2} & = 0 \\\\ 1 + 1 + 1 - \frac{V_\text{o}}{2} & = 0 \\\\ 3 - \frac{V_\text{o}}{2} & = 0 \\\\ \frac{V_\text{o}}{2} & = 3 \\\\ V_\text{o} & = 6 \text{V}\\\\ \end{align} \]

items.title: Overall description
items.text:
The image shows a classic three-op-amp instrumentation amplifier circuit. This configuration is widely used to precisely amplify small differential signals while rejecting common-mode noise.

The output voltage of this circuit is given by:

\[ V_\text{out} = (1 + \frac{2R_1}{R_\text{gain}})\frac{R_3}{R_2}(V_{2} - V_{1}) \]

items.title: Input Stage (Buffer and Gain Stage)
items.text:
Assuming ideal operational amplifiers with negative feedback:

• The virtual short condition dictates that the voltage at the inverting terminal of the top op-amp is \(V_{1}\).

• The voltage at the inverting terminal of the bottom op-amp is \(V_{2}\).

The current (\(I\)) flowing through the central resistor \(R_{\text{gain}}\) is driven by this voltage difference:

\[ I = \frac{V_1 - V_2}{R_\text{gain}} \]

Because the input terminals of an ideal op-amp draw zero current, this identical current \(I\) must also flow through both \(R_{1}\) resistors. Let \(V_{o1}\) be the output of the top op-amp and \(V_{o2}\) be the output of the bottom op-amp. Then:

\[ \begin{align} V_{o1}-V_{o2} & = I(R_{1}+R_{\text{gain}}+R_{1}) \\\\ V_{o1}-V_{o2} & = (\frac{1 + 2R_1}{R_\text{gain}})(V_1 - V_2) \\\\ \end{align} \]

items.title: Output Stage (Differential Amplifier)
items.text:
The second stage is a standard differential amplifier configuration with inputs \(V_{o1}\) and \(V_{o2}\):

\[ V_\text{out} = \frac{R_3}{R_2}(V_{o2} - V{o1}) \]

Substituting the relation from the first stage yields the final result:

\[ V_\text{out} = \frac{R_3}{R_2}(1 + \frac{2R_1}{R_\text{gain}})(V_2 - V_1) \]

items.title: Key Advantages
items.text:
• High Input Impedance: Signals \(V_{1}\) and \(V_{2}\) connect directly to the non-inverting terminals, offering extremely high loading impedance.

• Single-Resistor Gain Tuning: The overall differential gain can be adjusted seamlessly by varying only one component (\(R_{\text{gain}}\)) without disturbing resistor matching.

items.title: Ohm's Law
items.text:
Ohm's law defines resistance:

\[ R = \frac{V}{I} \]

where \(V\) is the voltage drop measured across an element, and \(I\) is the current through it.

Ohm's Law applies only to circuit elements where the resistance remain constant.

Examples where resistance does not remain constant:

  • lightbulbs (their resistance increases as they heat up)
  • diodes and transistors (not linear devices)

The Drude-Lorentz model, which describes the motion of electrons inside a conductor can be used to derive Ohm's Law.

items.title: Microscopic form of Ohm s Law
items.text:
The original form of Ohm's Law, \(R=V/I\), descrbied the macroscopic properties of resistive elements in a DC circuit.

A physical basis for this law was developed decades later (1900) by Paul Drude and refined by Hendrik Lorentz in 1905.

Their approach describes the motions of charged particles at the micro level, introducing the need for new terms:

  • Resistivity \(\rho\), and intrinsic material property.

  • Conductivity, \(1/\rho\).

  • Micrscopic current density, \(J = \sigma E\).
